# General

- Page: <https://kevintshoemaker.github.io/NRES-746/Week14_SpatialRegression.html>.
  Script: `CODE_Week14_SpatialRegression.R` (same seeds, same numbers).
- Monday, Nov. 23: spatial regression (first H1). No in-class WOD.
  *Spline by Hand* is due; go over it at the start of Tuesday, not
  Monday.
- Tuesday, Nov. 24: demo (second H1, ~50 min), hand out the take-home
  WOD *Neighbors* (due Mon., Nov. 30), then project work time. No Act,
  no lab key.
- Wednesday, Nov. 25: no class (Thanksgiving).
- One data set for the lecture and the demo: a simulated cheatgrass
  survey (say so), `data/CheatgrassSurvey.csv`, 200 plots in a 40 by
  30 km area, 77 burned (three fires), none in a roadless block.
  Truth: fire 0.5, elevation $-2$ per km, $\sigma_s = 0.7$,
  exponential with $\ell = 6$ km, $\sigma_e = 0.3$. Generator:
  `rcode/sim_Week14_cheatgrass.R` (seed 18).
- The seed was chosen for a clear contrast: this survey's `lm()` fire
  estimate (0.98) is two SDs above the truth. Across 70 other seeds it
  ran from $-0.04$ to 0.98. The 2000-survey simulation in section 1
  is the fair summary; don't present 0.98 as typical.
- The WOD uses a different data set (`data/SnowCourses.csv`). Push all
  three CSVs to `gh-pages` and check the URLs before Tuesday; the
  companion script and the WOD read them from the web.
- Packages students need to follow along: `sdmTMB`, `glmmTMB`, `mgcv`,
  `gstat`, `mvtnorm`. `INLA` is optional (large download, not on CRAN);
  show it on the projector.
- Questions on the page have no answers. *Land:* is where discussion
  should end up.
- Week 13's Gaussian process section got only a few minutes (Nov. 18),
  and the announcement promised more on GPs this week. Open Monday with
  a 3-min recap (MVN on $f$, kernel, length-scale; `gp_draws.html`
  with the squared exponential vs. exponential switch only), then let
  section 3 (`#gp-space`) carry the rest. If time is short, drop
  section 2's widget stops 4-5 to pay for it.
- Week 13's GAM discussion prompts weren't covered. Don't carry them
  over; Q1 (extrapolating to 32 °C) can come back on Tuesday as a
  one-line aside at the prediction maps, where the same caution applies
  outside the surveyed area.
- Tuesday's lecture is announced as "short," with project work after.
  Hold the demo to ~40 min if students are eager to start drafts (cut
  the Poisson bonus and the mesh-sensitivity details first).
- Rough drafts of final projects are due before Thanksgiving, and each
  student peer-reviews one other group's draft; explain the peer review
  on Monday or Tuesday (the announcement promised to).

# Part 1: Spatial regression (Monday, ~50 min)

No laptops needed. Seven sections is more than fits; the plan is
sections 1 and 3 in full, 2 and 4 briefly, 5 as a table, and 6 as far
as time allows. Whatever is left of 5 and 6 opens Tuesday.

**Nearby plots are alike (~10 min)**

- Workflow boxes MODELS and FIT: the new piece is in the noise model.
  Two district questions: the fire effect (a coefficient) and where to
  treat (a map).
- `lm()`: fire 0.98 (SE 0.11), elevation $-1.51$ (SE 0.19). Fire
  multiplies biomass by 2.7.
- Residual map, then the question.
- "`lm()` assumes the residuals are independent draws ... What on this
  map says otherwise? If an important covariate were missing ... what
  would its map look like?" *Land:* same-sign residuals cluster (blue
  patches in the southwest and the southeast corner; red along the
  northern edge and around easting 27, northing 6). A
  missing covariate would look like this map: smooth patches.
- Simulation: SD of the fire estimate across 2000 surveys 0.23; `lm()`
  reports 0.10; 95% intervals cover 59%. Board: 77 burned plots, 3
  fires. Link to the Two Cores WOD.
- The sandwich formula is a footnote; skip unless asked.

**The variogram (~7 min)**

- Board: semivariance is half the mean squared difference at distance
  $d$. Read the printed table: 0.20 at 1.3 km, 0.50 at 9 km, flat
  near 0.5 to 0.58 after.
- Name nugget, sill, range on the plot. Board:
  $\gamma(d) = \sigma_e^2 + \sigma_s^2(1 - \rho(d))$.
- Widget (`variogram.html`), stops in order (defaults: exponential,
  $\ell = 4$, $\sigma_s = 0.7$, $\sigma_e = 0.3$; nugget 0.09, sill
  0.58, correlation at 5 km 0.24, 0.13-distance 8.2 km):
    1. Nugget SD 0: dots match the background; curve starts at 0 (sill
       0.49).
    2. Nugget SD 0.8: dots speckle against the background; nugget 0.64,
       sill 1.13, correlation at 5 km down to 0.12. Ask what will
       change before moving it.
    3. Back to 0.3. $\ell = 1$: salt-and-pepper map, variogram flat by
       2 km (correlation at 5 km 0.01). $\ell = 10$: broad patches,
       still rising at 20 km (correlation 0.51).
    4. $\ell = 8$, "New landscape" 4-5 times: points beyond 12 km
       wander well off the curve.
    5. If time: Matérn at $\ell = 4$ (smoother patches; 0.13-distance
       11.7 km) and squared exponential (8.1 km).
- Q1 (nugget; length-scale and independent information) *Land:* the
  nugget adds plot-level noise the map can't show and lifts the whole
  curve. Most independent information at $\ell = 1$: plots farther
  apart than a few km are nearly independent, so 150 plots are close
  to 150 looks. At $\ell = 10$ the landscape has only a handful of
  independent patches.
- Q2 (new landscapes at 8 km) *Land:* the empirical variogram is noisy
  at long distances (few independent pairs), so a range read by eye is
  rough. Fit the model by likelihood.

**A Gaussian process over the map (~12 min; the core)**

- Board: $y = X\beta + s + \varepsilon$,
  $V = \sigma_s^2 e^{-D/\ell} + \sigma_e^2 I$. Then the three earlier
  $V$'s side by side: shared group, years apart, temperature gap. Now
  km apart.
- Walk through `nll_spatial()`: one new line (the `V` line).
- Results: fire 0.50 (SE 0.14), elevation $-1.44$ (SE 0.59),
  $\hat\sigma_s = 0.71$, $\hat\ell = 4.1$ km, $\hat\sigma_e = 0.27$;
  log-likelihood $-169.7$ against $-218.1$ (AIC 351.4 against 444.3).
- Three changes, in order: fire halves (within-neighborhood
  comparisons), its SE grows, elevation SE triples (smooth covariate
  against a smooth field).
- Fitted variogram curve over the `lm()` residual points.
- Matérn in two sentences: exponential is $\nu = 1/2$; the mesh
  packages use $\nu = 1$ and report a "range" where correlation is
  about 0.13, which is $2\ell$ for the exponential (8.2 km here).
  This is the likely sticking point when students compare outputs.
- Not on the page by design: the kriging code. The WOD asks for it.

**A mesh makes it fast (~8 min)**

- Cost: factoring $V$ took about 0.06 s for 1000 plots, 0.44 for 2000,
  3.6 for 4000 (numbers change a little each knit); about 8 min per
  evaluation at 20,000.
- Idea in one line: field = tent basis functions on a triangle mesh
  times vertex values; the vertex values get a Normal prior with a
  sparse precision matrix. Callbacks: degree-1 B-splines, and the
  tridiagonal precision of AR(1).
- Mesh figure: 131 vertices at `cutoff = 2`. One plot's three weights
  (0.46, 0.25, 0.29). $Q$ has about 17 nonzeros per row.
- Board summary: penalized spline = basis + prior on weights; GP =
  kernel; mesh field = a GP written the first way.
- Widget (`spatial_mesh.html`), stops (range 10 km): edge 15 (12
  vertices, correlation with the truth 0.32), 10 (20 vertices, 0.83),
  5 (63, 0.97), 3 (165, 0.996), 2 (336, 0.999). Then range 4 km: edge
  5 gives 0.53, 2 gives 0.975, 1 gives 0.998.
- Q (edge length and range) *Land:* little is gained below an edge of
  about a third of the range (10 km: edge 3; 4 km: edge 1.5 gives
  0.99). The edge has to be a fraction of the range, so the mesh
  depends on the field, not on the number of plots.

**One model, three packages (~6 min)**

- Show the three calls, then the table. `glmmTMB` matches `optim()`
  to four decimals in the log-likelihood ($-169.7104$).
- Table to read aloud: fire 0.50 / 0.50 / 0.55 / 0.54, all SE 0.14;
  range 8.2 / 8.2 / 8.9 / 9.8 km; $\sigma_e$ 0.27 for the exponential
  fits, 0.42 for the mesh fits (a smoother field and a finite mesh push
  fine-scale variation into the nugget).
- INLA: don't walk through the stack line by line. Say what the three
  pieces are (priors, the projection matrix, the stack) and that
  `inlabru` hides them. PC priors are stated as tail probabilities.
- Use the name table when students ask "which number is $\sigma_e$?"
  (`phi` in `sdmTMB`, a precision in INLA).

**The GAM alternative (~7 min)**

- `gam(... + s(x_km, y_km, k = 100), method = "REML")`: edf 53.6,
  fire 0.42 (SE 0.14). `bs = "gp"`: fire 0.48 (SE 0.14).
- Elevation: $-0.39$ (SE 3.9) with the thin plate smooth, $-1.54$
  (SE 2.4) with `bs = "gp"`, against $-1.44$ (SE 0.59) for the
  exponential field. Reason: both `mgcv` smooths leave planes
  unpenalized, and easting and northing explain 94% of elevation.
  `select = TRUE` only lowers the SE to 2.7.
- Three maps: fitted field's correlation with the true field 0.80;
  GAM smooth 0.59.
- "Which approach, when?" table: read three rows aloud (nuisance:
  GAM; want the range, or prediction away from data: random field;
  field changing through time: random field). The rest is reference
  for projects.
- Caveat to say out loud: in `bs = "gp"` the range is fixed in
  advance, not estimated.

**Discussion (if time; otherwise Tuesday)**

- Q1 (fire 0.98, SE 0.11, vs. 0.50, SE 0.14; "the field soaked up the
  fire effect") *Land:* the worry is legitimate in general (spatial
  confounding), and here the truth is 0.5, so the field removed bias,
  not signal. What identifies the fire effect is the contrast across
  fire boundaries between plots close enough to share the field. A
  better design pairs plots just inside and just outside each
  perimeter, and samples more fires.
- Q2 (elevation SE 0.19, 0.59, 3.9; estimates $-1.51$, $-1.44$,
  $-0.39$) *Land:* report the random field's estimate with its wide
  interval ($-2.6$ to $-0.3$) and say the survey can't separate
  elevation from other east-west gradients. The `lm()` SE is wrong for
  the same reason as the fire SE; the GAM's says the smooth and
  elevation are interchangeable. Truth is $-2$.
- Q3 (what to measure next) *Land:* open. Look where the field is
  strongly positive or negative (blue in the southwest and
  southeast corners, red around easting 27, northing 6) and ask what
  differs there: soil, grazing, seed source. If the new covariate is
  the right one, $\hat\sigma_s$ shrinks and the field map flattens.

**Skip if behind:** the variogram widget's stops 4-5, the mesh widget,
the INLA code, the "which approach" table (assign as reading).

# Part 2: A spatial analysis from start to finish (Tuesday, ~50 min)

Laptops open; students can run the script alongside. Start with a
5-min review of *Spline by Hand* (key in `wod/answer_keys/`) and
anything left from Monday's sections 5-6.

**Problem and candidate models (~5 min)**

- Workflow boxes PROBLEM and THEORIES. Threshold 60 g per square
  meter is log 4.09. M0 no field, M1 field, M2 field plus fire by
  elevation interaction.
- Practical points: project to km (`add_utm_columns()`), center
  covariates.

**The mesh (~6 min)**

- Table: cutoff 1, 2, 3 km give fire 0.53, 0.55, 0.49 (SE 0.14);
  range 8.6, 8.9, 6.2. Cutoff 5: log-likelihood falls from about
  $-172$ to $-187.7$. Cutoff 8: range 0.00, $\sigma_s$ 1633, a failed
  fit.
- "The 1-km mesh has almost twice the vertices ... What did the extra
  vertices buy? When would you need them?" *Land:* nothing here (same
  estimates, log-likelihood $-172.4$ vs. $-172.9$). They are needed
  when the range is short relative to 2 km, or plots are dense enough
  to show finer structure.

**Fit and check (~8 min)**

- `sanity(m1)`: nine green checks.
- QQ plot close to the line; standardized residual variogram: M0 rises
  from 0.4 to 1, M1 flat near 1.
- Say that this is the goodness-of-fit step of COMPARE.

**Compare (~12 min)**

- AIC: M0 444.3, M1 357.8, M2 359.8 ($\Delta$ 86.4, 0, 1.97). The
  interaction is $-0.08$ (SE 0.49): an uninformative parameter
  (Week 10).
- Cross-validation RMSE: random folds 0.730 (M0) vs. 0.538 (M1), 26%
  lower; 10-km blocks 0.794 vs. 0.784, a tie. Show the block map.
- Not on the page: `sdmTMB_cv()`'s summed log-likelihood makes M1 look
  much worse than M0 under blocks ($-358$ vs. $-244$), because it
  scores held-out points with the field's predicted value and
  $\sigma_e$ only, ignoring the field's uncertainty. Use RMSE, and
  don't show `$sum_loglik` without that caveat.
- "The district wants a map of the surveyed area, including the
  roadless block. Which of the two cross-validation results describes
  how well that map will do, and where ...?" *Land:* random folds
  describe cells with plots within a few km (most of the map); block
  folds describe the middle of the roadless block and anywhere beyond
  the survey edge.

**Predict (~12 min)**

- `predict()` columns: `est` = `est_non_rf` + `omega_s`. With `nsim`,
  one column per draw.
- Four maps. SE: mean 0.31 in the roadless block, 0.23 elsewhere,
  highest at the corners. Exceedance map: most of the northwest fire
  and a patch in the southeast fire are flagged; the northeast fire is
  not (high elevation).
- Truth check: RMSE over the grid 0.37 (M1) vs. 0.64 (M0). Of flagged
  cells, 81% are truly above the threshold; they include 67% of all
  cells that are.
- Kriging: name it, point to the Week 13 conditional-mean formula, and
  stop. The WOD has students code it.
- "The district can treat only a quarter of the area the map flags.
  ... highest predicted biomass, or the highest probability of
  exceeding the threshold?" *Land:* probability, if the goal is not to
  waste treatment. The rankings disagree where the SE is high: a cell
  far from plots can have a high prediction and a modest probability.
  A case for sampling there first.

**What we tell the district (~4 min)**

- Fire multiplies biomass by 1.7 (95% 1.3 to 2.3); `lm()` said 2.7.
  Elevation slope $-2.7$ to $-0.3$. Unmeasured variation with a range
  near 9 km and SD 0.64, as large as the fire effect.
- Corroborated against two rivals, not against a model with the
  missing covariate. REVISE: go measure it.

**Bonus, counts (~3 min if asked):** Poisson seedlings, fire 0.89
(SE 0.07) by `glm()`, 0.68 (SE 0.17) with the field; truth 0.5. Only
`family` changes.

**Hand out *Neighbors* (last 2 min).** Take-home, due Mon., Nov. 30.
Paper Parts 1-2, R for Parts 3-4, AI labels on each coding item.
Numbers they should get: Var of the mean $\sigma^2(1+\rho)/2$ (0.50,
0.75, 0.95; worth 2.00, 1.33, 1.05 stations); variogram nugget 10-30,
sill 100-120, range 15-25 km; `lm()` slope 31.6 (SE 5.9); `nll`
check 209.42; spatial slope 48.0 (SE 6.3), $\hat\sigma_s = 10.2$,
$\hat\ell = 11.8$ km, $\hat\sigma_e = 3.1$, log-likelihood $-206.92$
(same from `glmmTMB`); new site 43.7 cm from the regression part,
54.7 cm by kriging (station S28, 6.1 km away, residual $+26$ cm,
carries the most weight); prediction SE 8.1 cm, 10.6 far from the
network. Truth: slope 45, $\sigma_s = 8$, $\ell = 10$, $\sigma_e = 3$.
Key: `wod/answer_keys/`.

**Then:** project work time. Groups with spatial data: ask for their
coordinates' units, the number of locations, and whether space is the
question or a nuisance (the "which approach" table).
